summary.title: Implementing a Regular Expression Engine
summary.one_liner: You learn how regex patterns are parsed into postfix form, compiled into an epsilon-NFA with Thompson's construction, and matched by simulating the NFA in JavaScript.
takeaways: Finite automata (DFA, NFA, ε-NFA) are the theory behind regular expressions, and Kleene's theorem links them.
Thompson's construction builds an NFA from a regex by combining basis NFAs for ε and single symbols with union, concatenation and closure.
Regex is converted from infix to postfix after inserting explicit concatenation operators, then compiled with a stack.
Simulating the NFA by tracking a set of current states runs in O(n^2), far better than the exponential recursive backtracking approach.
DFAs give O(n) recognition but can suffer state explosion.
summary.summary: The article introduces finite automata (DFA, NFA, ε-NFA) and the theory connecting them to regular expressions. It then follows Ken Thompson's 1968 construction: a regex is preprocessed with explicit concatenation, converted to postfix notation, and compiled into an NFA using basis rules and inductive rules for union, concatenation and closure, with JavaScript code shown for each step. Finally it compares recursive backtracking with a state-set simulation of the NFA, including handling of ε-transitions, and puts the pieces together into a matcher.
